explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says the nations are “…bewildered by the roaring of the sea and the surging of the waves.” (Luke 21:25) So up in the sky there are signs, and down on the earth the water is making a whole lot of noise. My mixer on high speed has never made anybody that nervous.

Mountains are a good guess, but they aren't in this verse. Jesus says the nations are “…bewildered by the roaring of the sea and the surging of the waves.” (Luke 21:25) The shaking He mentions comes in the next verse, and it's the powers of the heavens that get shaken. Water is the answer here, baker.

Thunder and lightning sound like they'd fit, but Jesus doesn't say either one. What He says is that the nations are “…bewildered by the roaring of the sea and the surging of the waves.” (Luke 21:25) The noise is coming from the water down on the earth. Next time I'll read the verse before I let my imagination add a storm.

True, baker. Jesus says men “…will faint from fear and anxiety over what is coming upon the earth, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.” (Luke 21:26) That “for” ties the two together in His words. This is a heavy part of the passage.

This one is true, and that “for” in the verse is easy to skim past. Jesus says men “…will faint from fear and anxiety over what is coming upon the earth, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.” (Luke 21:26) So the shaking of the heavens is right there in His sentence. I think this is one of the heavier lines in the passage.

Yes, baker. That's Jesus describing His own coming. He says they will see “…the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory.” (Luke 21:27) When Jesus says Son of Man, He means Himself (Mark 2:10).

Gabriel doesn't show up in this verse, baker. Jesus says they will see “…the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory.” (Luke 21:27) When Jesus says Son of Man, He's talking about Himself (Mark 2:10). So the One in the cloud is Jesus.

No prophet is named in this verse, baker. Jesus says they will see “…the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory.” (Luke 21:27) When Jesus says Son of Man, He means Himself (Mark 2:10). So He's describing His own coming.

explanations.answer: Stand up and lift up your heads
explanations.explanation: That's right. Jesus says, “When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads…” (Luke 21:28) Right after talking about men fainting from fear, He tells His listeners to stand tall. I love that. That's a posture I wish my flour sacks had.

explanations.answer: Kneel down and cover your faces
explanations.explanation: Covering your face makes sense when things get scary, but that isn't what Jesus says. His words are, “When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads…” (Luke 21:28) Heads up, not faces covered. He tells them to stand, baker.

explanations.answer: Sit still and close your eyes
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't tell them to sit still or shut their eyes. He says, “When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads…” (Luke 21:28) That's standing and looking up, the opposite of ducking down. Eyes open, baker.

Right, baker. Jesus says to lift up your heads “…because your redemption is drawing near.” (Luke 21:28) That's the reason He gives for looking up instead of down. He doesn't say it's something to dread. It's something drawing near.

Punishment is a word that fits the fear in the verses before, but it isn't what Jesus says here. He says, “…stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” (Luke 21:28) He gives His listeners redemption as the reason to look up. I think that's worth lingering on.

Harvest is a good word, but you won't find it in this verse. Jesus says, “…stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” (Luke 21:28) Redemption is the word He picks, baker.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, “When they sprout leaves, you can see for yourselves and know that summer is near.” (Luke 21:30) Nobody has to explain it to you. You look at the tree and you just know.

Winter is the opposite direction. Jesus says that when the trees sprout leaves, “…you can see for yourselves and know that summer is near.” (Luke 21:30) New leaves point toward summer, baker. That's the whole picture in His parable.

No rainy season in this parable, baker. Jesus says, “When they sprout leaves, you can see for yourselves and know that summer is near.” (Luke 21:30) The leaves point to summer, and nobody needs a weather report. It's like peeking through my oven window: you can see for yourself when the cookies are golden.

That's the one. Jesus says, “So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.” (Luke 21:31) Leaves show summer is close, and these things happening show the kingdom of God is close. Same kind of seeing, baker.

Jesus doesn't name Elijah in this parable. He says, “So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.” (Luke 21:31) These things include what He just described, the Son of Man coming in a cloud (Luke 21:27). So the parable points to the kingdom of God being near, baker.

Rebuilding never comes up in this parable, baker. Jesus says, “So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.” (Luke 21:31) Leaves tell you summer is close, and these things tell you the kingdom is close. Even I can read that sign.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.” (Luke 21:33) Even heaven and earth don't outlast what He says. That's why I take His words so seriously, and why the ovens stay ready.

That's not it, and the temple is what started this whole conversation. The disciples asked when it would be thrown down (Luke 21:5-7). Here Jesus says, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.” (Luke 21:33) His words outlast even heaven and earth, baker.

Jesus doesn't say the city lasts forever here. He says, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.” (Luke 21:33) The contrast is between heaven and earth passing away and His words that never will. The city isn't named in that sentence, baker.

Right, baker. Jesus says, “But watch yourselves, or your hearts will be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life…” (Luke 21:34) Worries of life are right there in His list, next to the other two. I think a lot of us know that one well.

Money is a fair thing to worry about, but Jesus doesn't name it in this verse. He says, “…your hearts will be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life…” (Luke 21:34) The third thing on His list is the worries of life. Everyday stuff, baker.

Jesus doesn't list that here. His words are, “…your hearts will be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life…” (Luke 21:34) Praise might feel good, but it never makes the list. The third item is the worries of life, the kind that follow you around like flour on an apron, baker.

That's right. Jesus says, “…that day will spring upon you suddenly like a snare.” (Luke 21:34) A snare doesn't send a warning before it catches. Then He adds, “For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of all the earth.” (Luke 21:35)
A sunrise gives you a long warning, and Jesus picks a different picture. He says, “…that day will spring upon you suddenly like a snare.” (Luke 21:34) Suddenly is His word, baker. Not slowly.

Jesus doesn't call it quiet. He says, “…that day will spring upon you suddenly like a snare.” (Luke 21:34) The word He uses is suddenly, and the picture is a snare. I'd call that anything but a whisper, baker.

This one is False, and it's an easy one to miss. Jesus says, “For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of all the earth.” (Luke 21:35) That's every person on the earth, not just one city. He means all of us, baker.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, “For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of all the earth.” (Luke 21:35) It isn't only about the people of Jerusalem. It reaches everyone who lives on the earth.

Yes, baker. Jesus says to pray “…that you may have the strength to escape all that is about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man.” (Luke 21:36) Stand is His word. After all the fainting and fear, He's talking about standing before Him.

Hiding makes sense when things get scary, but Jesus doesn't say it. He says to pray “…that you may have the strength to escape all that is about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man.” (Luke 21:36) The word is stand. No hiding in this verse, baker.

Jesus doesn't use that word here. He says to pray “…that you may have the strength to escape all that is about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man.” (Luke 21:36) The word is stand. It's the same word as the earlier "…stand up and lift up your heads…" baker.

That's it, baker. The writer says, “Every day Jesus taught at the temple, but every evening He went out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives.” (Luke 21:37) Temple by day, Mount of Olives by night. That's a steady routine.

That's not where the writer puts Him in this verse. He says, “Every day Jesus taught at the temple, but every evening He went out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives.” (Luke 21:37) So the evenings were on the Mount of Olives. No house is named, baker.

Capernaum isn't named here. The writer says, “Every day Jesus taught at the temple, but every evening He went out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives.” (Luke 21:37) Temple by day, Mount of Olives by night. Quite the daily commute, baker.
Yes, baker. The writer says, “And early in the morning all the people would come to hear Him at the temple.” (Luke 21:38) All of them, and early. I can barely get to my own ovens that fast.

Only the disciples would be a much smaller crowd than the verse describes. The writer says, “And early in the morning all the people would come to hear Him at the temple.” (Luke 21:38) It's all the people, not just one small group. Quite the crowd, baker.

The text doesn't narrow it down to one group. The writer says, “And early in the morning all the people would come to hear Him at the temple.” (Luke 21:38) That's all the people, so the scribes aren't the only ones heading there. That's an early crowd even my busiest bakery morning can't match, baker.
